claims.title: Shopper order data may be readable in transit to the storefront API
claims.description: `flow:entity:shopper>process:storefront-api>place-order` crosses from `boundary:public-internet` to `boundary:storefront-dmz` and carries shopper PII and financial order data, including shipping addresses and card last-four, but its `encryption_in_transit` state is unknown. If transport encryption is not enforced for this browser-facing flow, an on-path attacker on the public route can intercept submitted orders before they reach `process:storefront-api`. The captured shopper identifiers and order details can subsequently be used to target accounts and purchases handled by the storefront.

severity.justification: Likelihood is high conditional on the unknown transport setting because `flow:entity:shopper>process:storefront-api>place-order` crosses the public-internet boundary and can be observed by attackers able to position themselves on that route. Impact is high because the flow carries `pii` and `financial` order information for shoppers, and intercepted personal data cannot be recalled.

mitigations.summary: Require modern TLS for shopper checkout traffic
mitigations.detail: Configure and verify TLS 1.2+ for `flow:entity:shopper>process:storefront-api>place-order`, redirect or reject plaintext requests, and record the verified transport setting in the model.

mitigations.summary: Minimize payment-related fields in the request
mitigations.detail: Avoid carrying payment-related values beyond what checkout requires and use opaque order references where downstream processing can resolve them.

claims.title: Settlement callback details may be exposed on the processor-to-storefront path
claims.description: `flow:entity:card-processor>process:storefront-api>settlement-webhook` crosses from `boundary:public-internet` to `process:storefront-api` and carries a financial settlement confirmation, while both its protocol and `encryption_in_transit` state are unknown. If the callback is delivered without verified transport encryption, an on-path observer can intercept settlement status and order-related payment information. Those observations identify paid orders and can help an attacker target subsequent shopper or order-processing activity.

severity.justification: Likelihood is high conditional on the unknown transport settings because the webhook traverses the public-internet boundary into internet-facing `process:storefront-api`. Impact is medium because the flow is tagged `financial` and reveals payment-settlement information, but the model describes a settlement confirmation rather than the full order corpus.

mitigations.detail: Require HTTPS with current TLS for `flow:entity:card-processor>process:storefront-api>settlement-webhook` and document the negotiated transport protection.
Use an opaque settlement or order reference in the callback and resolve sensitive payment detail only through authenticated processor-side retrieval.

claims.title: Order details may be readable between the storefront DMZ and order service
claims.description: `flow:process:storefront-api>process:order-service>submit-order` crosses from `boundary:storefront-dmz` to `boundary:core-services` and carries order contents, shopper identifiers, and shipping addresses. Its `encryption_in_transit` state is unknown. If this gRPC transport is unencrypted, an attacker able to observe the DMZ-to-core path can intercept PII and financial order information. The identifiers and addresses disclosed on this path can then be correlated with records handled by `store:orders-db`. This is conditional on the unresolved transport setting, not an assertion that gRPC is plaintext.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium conditional on unknown encryption: the attacker needs a position on the DMZ-to-core path, but the flow is a stated boundary crossing and no transport protection is verified. Impact is high because the flow carries both `pii` and `financial` order data, including shopper identifiers and addresses.

mitigations.summary: Enforce mTLS on the storefront-to-order-service gRPC call
mitigations.detail: Set `encryption_in_transit` on `flow:process:storefront-api>process:order-service>submit-order` to mutually authenticated TLS so confidentiality and service peer verification apply across the boundary.

mitigations.summary: Send opaque order references where feasible
mitigations.detail: Keep raw shopper identifiers and addresses out of the cross-zone message when `process:order-service` can retrieve required details through a separately protected path.

claims.title: Order database traffic may expose the order corpus if transport encryption is absent
claims.description: `flow:process:order-service>store:orders-db>read-write-orders` carries order rows, shipping addresses, and card last-four to `store:orders-db`, whose assets include `pii` and `financial`; both the protocol and `encryption_in_transit` state are unknown. If this database connection is unencrypted, an attacker with a foothold on the core-services network path can intercept records as `process:order-service` reads or writes them. Captured order identifiers and customer details support targeted abuse of the order-processing and shopper-facing paths.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium conditional on the unknown database transport configuration because interception requires a core-services network position, but no protocol or encryption control is verified. Impact is high because `store:orders-db` is confidential and holds `pii` and `financial` data, including shipping addresses and card last-four.

mitigations.summary: Require encrypted and authenticated database sessions
mitigations.detail: Configure TLS for `flow:process:order-service>store:orders-db>read-write-orders`, require certificate validation, and record the actual protocol and encryption posture.
Segment the database connection path and permit the order-service identity only, reducing the systems capable of passively observing the connection.

claims.title: Receipt transfer confidentiality is unresolved by conflicting TLS statements
claims.description: The model states `encryption_in_transit` is absent on `flow:process:order-service>store:receipt-archive>append-receipt`, which carries receipts recording completed orders, but the source states that this path is on TLS. If the model's absent setting reflects the deployed path, an attacker able to observe the order-service-to-archive connection can intercept receipt contents and learn completed-order activity; if the source is correct, TLS should prevent that disclosure. The discrepancy itself must be resolved rather than treating either statement as a verified control.

quotes.text:
That is on TLS with the order service's own
service account

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium because the model states transport encryption is absent, although the contrary TLS source assertion makes exploitation conditional on resolving that conflict; an attacker still needs access to the internal path. Impact is medium because the receipt flow records completed-order activity and can expose business-sensitive order information.

mitigations.summary: Reconcile and verify the receipt-transfer TLS configuration
mitigations.detail: Test the deployed connection for certificate validation and current TLS, correct the contradictory model and source records, and reject any plaintext connection to `store:receipt-archive`.

mitigations.summary: Reduce receipt data on the transport path
mitigations.detail: Store only an opaque order reference in receipt-transfer metadata where the archive does not require detailed order content.

claims.title: Orders database copies expose confidential shopper data if at-rest encryption is absent
claims.description: `store:orders-db` is classified confidential, holds `pii` and `financial` assets, and has `encryption_at_rest` state unknown. If this unresolved setting means its PostgreSQL storage, operational snapshots, or decommissioned media are not encrypted, an attacker who obtains a storage-layer copy can read order rows, shipping addresses, and card last-four without authenticating through `process:order-service`. The disclosed customer and order data can then be used to target shopper accounts and purchases. This is conditional on the unknown at-rest encryption state, not a claim that the database is presently unencrypted.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium conditional on the unknown `encryption_at_rest` value: obtaining a storage copy requires access to an operational copy or media, but no at-rest protection is verified. Impact is high because `store:orders-db` is classified confidential and contains both `pii` and `financial` order data.

mitigations.summary: Verify and enforce database encryption at rest
mitigations.detail: Establish the actual `encryption_at_rest` setting for `store:orders-db`, then require managed-key or customer-managed-key encryption for the primary database and all snapshots, backups, and replicas.
Limit export, snapshot, and restore permissions to separate least-privileged principals and restrict decrypt permissions to the database service path.

claims.title: Receipt archive copies may reveal completed-order records if the stated encryption conflict resolves to no protection
claims.description: `store:receipt-archive` has `encryption_at_rest` state absent in the model, while the source states that the bucket is encrypted with a customer-managed key. If the absent model setting reflects the actual archive or any operational copy of it, an attacker holding a bucket export, backup, or storage-layer copy can read receipt records without using the order service's service account. Those records identify completed orders and can expose business-sensitive order activity. This draft is conditional on resolving the contradictory at-rest encryption statements.

quotes.text: the bucket is encrypted with a customer-managed key.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium because the model records absent at-rest encryption but the source asserts a customer-managed key, so the scenario depends on resolving that conflict and obtaining a storage copy. Impact is medium because the archive contains one receipt per completed order and therefore discloses business-sensitive order records.

mitigations.summary: Reconcile and continuously verify bucket encryption
mitigations.detail: Confirm that `store:receipt-archive` uses the stated customer-managed key in the deployed bucket and correct the contradictory model value; enforce the same key policy for every backup or exported copy.
Separate principals allowed to read objects, export objects, and use the customer-managed key, and audit bulk archive reads and exports.

claims.title: A recovered order-service database password enables bulk reads of orders
claims.description: The application account used by `process:order-service` on `flow:process:order-service>store:orders-db>read-write-orders` has full read/write access to `store:orders-db`, and its password is kept in an environment variable on the worker. An attacker who recovers that standing credential from the worker's environment can use it to query the confidential orders database and read the full corpus of shopper addresses, order records, and card last-four values. The second-order impact is corpus-scale disclosure: one recovered password reaches data for all shoppers rather than only the order associated with a particular request.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium because recovering an environment-held password requires access to `process:order-service` or an exposure path for its environment, but the credential is a static worker environment variable. Impact is high because the application account has full read/write access to confidential `store:orders-db`, which contains `pii` and `financial` data.

mitigations.detail: Use workload identity or short-lived database credentials issued from a dedicated secret manager rather than storing the application-account password in the worker environment.

mitigations.summary: Reduce the application account's database scope
mitigations.detail: Replace the full read/write grant with narrowly scoped roles, rows, columns, and operations required by `process:order-service`, so one recovered credential cannot read the full corpus.
Audit and alert on bulk or unusual queries made by the application account, especially reads exceeding normal order-processing volume.
